Additionally, the in vivo anti-adhesion barrier and wound healing efficiency in Oxaliplatin · Colorectal cancer Introduction The main treatment of colorectal cancer is usually surgical removal of the tumor (Dinh et al. Surgical cuts during the operation result in a wound in the abdominal cavity of the patient.
Wound healing naturally occurs due to cell proliferation and tissue regeneration.

The wound healing process includes 4 stages: hemostasis and blood clotting; inflammation; cell growth and proliferation; and tissue regeneration, remodeling, and strengthening (Schultz et al. These integrated and overlapping stages are influenced by intrinsic and extrinsic factors and often result in unwanted adhesions of tissues.

Surgical wounds may lead to adhesions between the wound and the healthy surrounding tissue, inflammation, and organ dysfunction (Menzies et al. Following abdominal surgery, more than 95% of patients experienced adhesion and chronic pain despite the improvements in surgical techniques and technologies (Weibel et al. 1973, Lauder et al. In clinical settings, hydrogels are widely used to create a physical barrier which prevents adhesions.
Hydrogel anti-adhesion barriers help reduce adhesions by mechanical separation of damaged tissue surfaces during the wound repair in the abdominal cavity.
In addition, the hydrogel polymeric matrix is made up of multiple interconnected polymer chains, and therefore can be used as a drug delivery system.
Drug and bioactive compounds (active pharmaceutical ingredients) can be encapsulated within the porous matrix and delivered on-site where the tumor was removed.

Oxaliplatin is a platinum-based anti-cancer drug that can bind to nucleophilic molecules and form DNA intra-strand adducts inhibiting DNA transcription (Alcindor et al. Sanofi-Aventis markets Oxaliplatin under the trademark Eloxatin®.
Although oxaliplatin can be applied to various types of cancer, it is frequently used as the second-line treatment of colorectal cancer.
The drug is available in the market as an intravenous solution formulation of 1 to 5 mg/ mL of oxaliplatin in water having a pH range of 4.5 to 6.

Oxaliplatin is also one of the most frequently selected for hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (de Jong et al. In the past, we succeeded in preparing hydrogels for the prevention of postoperative abdominal adhesion and colorectal cancer therapy (Lee et al. 2019; Dinh et al. 20 and confirmed the pharmacokinetic profile and anti-adhesive effect of oxaliplatin-loaded hydrogels (Abuzar et al. 20 for the prevention of postoperative abdominal adhesion and colorectal cancer therapy.
We recognize a growing demand for anti-adhesion solutions or gels suitable for postsurgical uses.
Commercial hyaluronic acid and poloxamer hydrogels are not able to adhere to and maintain a physical barrier over an extended time.

Meanwhile, polysaccharides present a potential solution to this challenge by enhancing muco-adhesiveness. (Lee et al. Our secondary purpose is to provide in situ oxaliplatin for additional local antitumor effects when the hydrogel is applied at the tumor site.

Moreover, hydrophilic oxaliplatin can be incorporated into hydrogels effectively (Dinh et al. In this current study, oxaliplatin-loaded chitosan-pectin-sodium alginate hydrogel scaffolds were prepared and evaluated in vitro and in vivo for their wound healing efficacy.
A major consideration in synthesizing a hydrogel system for post-operative colorectal cancer treatment is to employ suitable polymers.
The hydrogel should be non-toxic, biocompatible with human tissues, and biodegradable at the ideal rate corresponding to the release of the drug.
Between biodegradable synthetic, natural, and natural-derived polymers, we are especially interested in the natural groups due to their higher biocompatibility and lower toxicity.

Cationic Journal of Pharmaceutical Investigation (20 54:857–871 chitosan can form polyelectrolyte complexes with anionic polymers in low-pH environments (Ahmadi et al. Pectin is an anionic polysaccharide composed of D-galacturonic acid with methoxylated carboxyl groups, found in the cell walls of many terrestrial plants (Lara-Espinoza et al. Alginic acid is a naturally occurring compound of edible β-d-mannuronic acid and α-l-guluronic acid residues, which can be transformed into unbranched, unarranged polysaccharides called alginates in the presence of alkaline metals (Bertagnolli et al. In this current study, the formation of chitosan, pectin, and sodium alginate into polyelectrolyte complexes is simply based on physical interaction of the monomers, with no additional chemical agent.
The complex was expected to possess higher mechanical strength compared to single-polymer systems.

Depending on the patient, the target tumor site, and the wound, an ideal wound dressing hydrogel can carry an accurate, specific dose of anti-cancer drug. 3D printing technology can be used to develop customized drug delivery systems; thus, a 3D-printed hydrogel can provide a “tailor-made” solution that fits a patient’s requirements.

In this study, the Syringe Bio-Dispenser (Dr. INVIVO 4D, ROKIT Healthcare, Seoul, Republic of Korea), a mechanical piston-based dispensing system, was employed to print out the chitosan-pectin-sodium alginate scaffolds using the exact volume of dose-specific drug-loaded hydrogels.
In this study, we designed and developed a biodegradable, biocompatible 3D-printed hydrogel for wound dressing and drug delivery applications.

Oxaliplatin loaded-chitosan-pectin-sodium alginate hydrogels were prepared by self-assembly technique by dissolving oxaliplatin in water, then adding the solution into the hydrogel aqueous systems. 3D printing of hydrogels A scaffold model (2.5 mm × 2.5 mm × 1.0 mm) was designed using NewCreator K (Version 1.57.80, Rokit Healthcare, Seoul, Republic of Korea) and exported as an STL file.

Experimental design Design of experiment (DoE) has been widely used for the design of multi-factor experiments to provide efficient data collection.
The experimental design was performed by JMP® software (version 17.0.0; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA).

Statistical analysis was performed by using JMP® software to identify the optimal process parameters of the 3D printer with 5 factors: X1 (chitosan-to-pectin ratio), X2 (fill density, %), X3 (print speed, mm/s), X4 (Core nozzle, GA) and X5 (the presence of SA in the formulation) (Table 2).
The chitosan-to-pectin ratio was selected as categorical and chitosan-to-pectin ratios of 1, 2, and 3 were used as 3 categories.
Core nozzles were selected as categorical and 20, 22, and 25 GA nozzles were used as 3 categories.
The presence of SA was selected as conditional categorical, with (yes) and without (no) were used as 2 categories.
Fill density and print speed are 2 continuous variables.

The D-optimal design was used to optimize and evaluate the main effects, interaction effects and quadratic effects of the process permeates on the responses, Y1 (area accuracy, %), Y2 (height, mm), Y3 (length, mm), and Y4 (width, mm) (Table 3).

In vitro drug release The in vitro release of 5-FU and oxaliplatin from hydrogels was studied in PBS (pH = 7..
The hydrogels were inserted into a Float-A-Lyzer™ Dialysis device (10 K MWCO) with 1 mL PBS buffer and placed in a tube containing 25 mL PBS buffer.

In vivo evaluation of intraperitoneal 3D-printed gel scaffolds All experiments were approved by the IACUC at Yonsei University, Seoul, Republic of Korea, and were performed according to the IACUC guidelines, approval code: IACUC- A202301–1609-01, approval date: 19th January 2023.
The anti-adhesion barrier efficacy of the hydrogels was evaluated in male SD rats.
Male SD rats aged seven weeks were randomly divided into groups (n = 3).
Briefly, the rats were anesthetized with isoflurane.
During anesthetization, a ventral midline incision approximately 5 cm in length was made on the abdomen of the rat to open the abdominal cavity.
After the peritoneum was carefully handled with forceps and opened, on the left abdominal sidewall a 4 × 4 injury was made with a biopsy punch.
Rats were then treated according to their group with either 1 dose of hydrogel or 1 gel scaffold (approximately 0.2 mL of hydrogel containing 0.8 mg 5-FU and 0.3 mg oxaliplatin).
Each formulation was prepared at a dose of 4 mg/kg 5-FU and 1.5 mg/kg oxaliplatin.
At the end of the surgery, the abdominal layers and skin incisions were closed completely.
Rats were put back in their cages and the same care regime that was provided before the surgery was continued.
All surgeries were performed by the same individual.
After 7 days, the rats were anesthetized and sacrificed, and the abdominal cavity was opened again to reveal the treated wounded region.
The wound healing and anti-adhesion efficacy of the hydrogels were evaluated.
The anti-adhesion efficacy of the hydrogel system was scored.
To prevent bias, the researcher who assigned the anti-adhesion efficiency scores was blinded to the study and did not participate in performing the surgeries.

The in vivo evaluation of the intraperitoneal anti-adhesion effect was performed three times, during which the three researchers who scored the adhesion formations worked separately and were all blinded to the study.
Cell viability assay A cell viability assay was performed to access the cytotoxicity of the hydrogels.

The NIH-3T3 fibroblast (Korea Cell Line Bank, Republic of Korea) and Cellosaurus CCD- 1064SK human skin (ThermoFisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) cell lines were chosen as model cell lines to evaluate the toxicity of the hydrogels without oxaliplatin.

NIH-3T3 fibroblast cells were seeded at a density of 5 × 104 cells/well in a 96-well plate and incubated in Dulbecco’s modified Eagle’s medium (DMEM) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) at 37 °C with 5% CO for 24 h. Following cell incubation, the culture medium was replaced with a medium containing the hydrogels.

And the cells were cultured for an additional 24 h. Cell viability was assessed using the WST-1 assay, which employs a water-soluble tetrazolium salt to generate a water-soluble formazan dye by reduction in the presence of mitochondrial dehydrogenases.
Absorbance was measured at 450 nm (reference wavelength, 625 nm) using a microplate reader (Infinite 200 PRO, Tecan, Männedorf, Switzerland).

CCD-1064SK human skin cells were seeded at a density of 10,000 cells/well in a 96-well plate and incubated in Iscove’s Modified Dulbecco’s Medium (IMDM) supplemented with 10% FBS at 37 °C with 5% CO for 24 h. Cell proliferation was assessed using the CCK-8 assays using a BioTek Cytation 5 Cell Imaging Multimode Reader (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA).

Results and discussion Optimization of oxaliplatin solution at various pH Oxaliplatin is very soluble in water (pH = 7) (9.69 mg/mL).
Oxaliplatin contains a diamino cyclohexane and an oxalate ring.
During hydrolysis, the ring opens, and water replaces both molecules, releasing a monodentate oxalato ligand.

This ring-opening is reversible, thus making oxaliplatin “semi-stable” at neutral pH as it oscillates between the ring and water-bonded forms (Lucas et al. As a result of this pH dependent behavior, oxaliplatin is pH sensitive, and therefore the solubility of oxaliplatin and the stability of the ions at different pH were tested (Schridde et al. In aqueous phosphate buffer solutions at 25 °C, at high pH (pH = 7., the solubility of oxaliplatin was lower (7.68 mg/mL) compared to that of oxaliplatin at lower pH values (Table 5).

This finding agrees with previous studies which showed that at pH 7.4, the value K of oxaliplatin was highest when in interaction with a pH-responsive receptor, and the K values decreased when pH values decreased (Xiao et al. 2012; Li et al. At high K the dissociation products are highly created, therefore forming complexation is more likely.

The high solubility of oxaliplatin at low pH compared to pH 7.4, agrees with Xiao et al. who reported oxaliplatin released more rapidly at pH 4.5 than at pH 7.4 (Xiao et al. Once oxaliplatin is released from the hydrogel system, it can passively target cancerous environments (Chu et al. A previous study by Mehta et al. demonstrates that oxaliplatin at low concentrations (below 1 mg/mL) shows low oxaliplatin-complexation stability, and that chloride anions lead to the decomposition of oxaliplatin (Mehta et al. 20, thus oxaliplatin interaction with carrier and/or media was concerned.
The addition of acetic acid in hydrogel aqueous solutions of oxaliplatin might be critical.
However, no change in pH was observed during a week at pH 4.5 adjusted by acetic acid at 25 °C (Table 6).

Thermo-reversible gelation of pectin and chitosan mixture was investigated and confirmed by Nordby et al. (Nordby et al. According to the report, the value r was calculated as Eq. (1).
The value of gelation temperature depends on the composition of the pectin and chitosan.

In the range of 0.25 ≤ r ≤ 0.75, the gelation temperature rises with increasing r. With low pectin contents, temperature reduction is required to form a gel network, in contrast, with high pectin contents, cross-links emerge at high temperatures.
In this current study, low pectin contents were studied, and different pectin-to-chitosan ratios (1: 1, 1: 2, and 1: 3 w/w) with or without the addition of sodium alginate were tested (Table 1).

Conclusion A 3D-printed biodegradable physically cross-linked chitosan-pectin-sodium alginate scaffold was developed for wound dressing applications.
The C2P1NaA scaffolds showed good printability and the final lyophilized ones exhibited good physical integrity and flexibility.
Optimization of the 3D-printing process was performed.

Oxaliplatin was successfully loaded into hydrogels to improve intraperitoneal chemotherapy alongside anti-adhesion barrier function as a clinical outcome; furthermore, we observed sustained release of oxaliplatin from the formulated hydrogels.
However, oxaliplatin pharmacokinetics, along with toxicity, cytotoxicity, and cell viability studies for this novel system are yet to be performed.

The current study results indicate that the freeze-dried 3D-printed oxaliplatin-loaded C2P1NaA scaffolds could be used as a suitable candidate for wound dressings and local anti-tumor effects in advanced colorectal cancer treatment.
